content.text: A Trie (pronounced "try"), also known as a prefix tree, is a tree-based data structure that stores a dynamic set of strings, commonly used for searching words and prefixes efficiently. Each node represents a character, and words are stored by linking characters together from the root to leaf nodes.

items: Efficient Prefix Searching: Tries allow for quick lookups of words and prefixes, making them ideal for autocomplete and dictionary applications.
Hierarchical Character Storage: Unlike hash maps or arrays, tries store characters in a tree structure, reducing redundancy.
Supports Various Operations: Tries efficiently handle operations like searching, insertion, deletion, and prefix matching.
No Collisions: Unlike hash tables, tries do not suffer from collisions, making lookup times more predictable.
Memory Usage: Tries can consume more memory due to pointers at each node but optimize storage for shared prefixes.
A root node (starting point of all words).
Child nodes representing characters.
A boolean flag at the end of a word to mark completion.

items: Trie Nodes Store Characters:

Fast Lookups: Searching for words and prefixes takes O(m) time.
No Collisions: Unlike hash maps, tries avoid key collisions.
Efficient Prefix Matching: Ideal for autocomplete and dictionary applications.
Space Optimization: Common prefixes are stored once, reducing redundancy.
High Memory Usage: Requires extra storage for child node pointers.
Inefficient for Short Strings: If strings are short, a hash table may be more space-efficient.
Slower than Hash Tables for Exact Matches: Hash maps provide O(1) lookups, while tries take O(m).

items: A Trie is a tree-based data structure used for storing words efficiently.
It supports O(m) time complexity for searching, inserting, and prefix matching.
Commonly used in autocomplete, dictionaries, spell checking, and network routing.
Advantages include fast prefix lookups and no hash collisions.
Limitations include high memory usage and slower exact lookups compared to hash tables.
